message.content:
The two unknown side‑lengths \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy  

\[
\begin{cases}
2(x+y)=14 \quad &(\text{perimeter})\\[4pt]
xy=15          \quad &(\text{area})
\end{cases}\Longrightarrow 
\begin{cases}
x+y=7 \\[4pt]
xy=15 .
\end{cases}
\]

Treat one variable as a root of a quadratic equation.  
From \(x+y=s=7,\ xy=p=15\),

\[
t^{\,2}-st+p=t^{\,2}-7t+15=0 .
\]

Its discriminant is  

\[
D=s^{2}-4p=7^{2}-4(15)=49-60=-11<0 .
\]

Because the discriminant is **negative**, this quadratic has *no real roots*. Hence there are **no real numbers** \(x>0,\;y>0\) satisfying both conditions simultaneously.

---

### Bottom line
A rectangle whose perimeter equals 14 units and whose area equals 15 square units does **not exist** in Euclidean geometry. Any attempt to find “length” and “width” would lead to imaginary numbers rather than physical dimensions.
